## Results

Evaluation on the historical window (through October 2008), 10% sample of the
characters, ROC AUC per test month:

| Definition | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All rows (`only_prev_active=False`, old) | 0.50 | 0.55 | 0.75 | 0.79 | 0.79 | 0.83 | 0.79 |
| Characters active in `M - 1`, default hyperparameters | — | 0.82 | 0.82 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.87 | 0.88 |
| Characters active in `M - 1`, tuned | 0.89 | 0.87 | 0.86 | 0.87 | 0.87 | 0.89 | 0.89 |

The three rows score different populations or different pipelines, so they are
not directly comparable. The near-chance first folds of the old definition do not
appear with the current one, and the rows with `prev_played` false are not "easy"
— they have no features, so the model cannot rank them (AUC 0.43 to 0.80 within
that group). Compared on the same test rows, training on all rows gave 0.64 to
0.82, against 0.82 to 0.90 when training on active rows only.

The tuned row is the mean over the 30 folds of the final configuration, described
below. It is optimistic: the search ran on these same folds.

These numbers change by a few hundredths between runs: `sample_by_user` is
seeded, but the model itself is not.

## The tuned configuration

The search ran in three stages, each with its own Optuna study, each stage's
winner carried into the next through `frozen=`. All three ran on a 10% sample of
the characters; the final fit uses every character.

| Stage | Choices | Model | Trials | Best AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `features` (2% sample) | the eight feature-table choices | HGB, defaults | 40 | 0.8599 |
| `gaps` (10%) | `session_gap`, `zone_session_gap`, `use_class_features` | logreg | 18 | 0.8591 |
| `structural` (10%) | the six post-feature-table choices | logreg | 40 | 0.8694 |
| `capacity` (10%) | the four HGB hyperparameters | HGB | 60 | 0.8808 |

The winning configuration:

| Group | Values |
|---|---|
| Feature table | `session_gap=60`, `zone_session_gap=same`, `lags=(1,2,3)`, `diff_lags=(1,2)`, location on, Gini off, monthly on, class on |
| Structural | `drop_month`, `cardinality_threshold=17`, `drop_null_fraction=0.9061` |
| Model | HGB, `learning_rate=0.0344`, `max_leaf_nodes=54`, `min_samples_leaf=163`, `l2_regularization=0.0037` |

Three findings are worth pulling out.

**Lags matter most.** Dropping them entirely costs about 1.5 AUC points, the
largest single effect in the whole search. The monthly per-character block and
the location block each add about 0.5.

**`learning_rate` dominates the model search**, with a correlation of −0.908
against the score. The best value, 0.034, sits at the bottom of the range the
search was given (0.02–0.3), which means the optimum is probably below it. The
default of 0.1 was roughly three times too high.

**Two choices turned out to be flat** and could be dropped from the space:
`cardinality_threshold` (correlation −0.021) and `l2_regularization` (+0.009).

### `char` is account age, not identity

The structural search produced a result that looked wrong: dropping the `char`
column cost 0.019 AUC, the largest effect anywhere. The obvious reading — the
model memorises individual characters — is not what happens.

`char` is an `Int32`, and `TableVectorizer` passes numeric columns through
unchanged, so the model sees a raw integer rather than a one-hot identity. And
character ids are assigned sequentially at creation, so the id is a near-perfect
proxy for account age: Spearman correlation with the character's first observed
month is **0.9986**.

Account age is a strong churn predictor on its own:

| Tenure (months) | Churn rate |
|---|---|
| 1 | 0.671 |
| 2 | 0.362 |
| 3 | 0.278 |
| 6 | 0.243 |
| 12 | 0.186 |

`first_month` was never in the feature table — it is in `add_lagged_features`'s
`exclude_cols` — so the model had no explicit age signal and read it off the id.

Adding `tenure` as an explicit feature confirms the diagnosis. With tenure
present, on the same folds:

| Feature set | AUC |
|---|---|
| `char` kept | 0.8716 |
| `char` dropped | **0.8730** |

The 0.019 AUC that `char` appeared to carry was account age. Once tenure is
explicit, the id adds nothing and dropping it is marginally better.

## Held-out evaluation on unseen files

The most distinctive part of the design is that the plan is fitted once and then
run on files it has never seen, parsing included. Two windows make that work:

- `HISTORICAL_END = 2008-10-31` — everything up to and including October 2008 is
  training material.
- `UNSEEN_START = 2008-10-01` and `UNSEEN_END = 2009-01-10` — the unseen window.

The two overlap by one month on purpose. November's features are built from
October's activity, so if the unseen window started in November, the first month
it could score would have no features at all. The overlap gives the unseen run
one month of history to work from.

`fit_final` fits the whole graph — parsing included — on the historical files
using every character, and saves the learner with joblib. `score_unseen` loads
that saved learner and calls `.predict()` with the unseen environment. The same
code path parses files it has never seen, which is the point: there is no
separate pre-processing script that could drift from the training one.

Splitting the two matters because the fit is the expensive half. Once the learner
is on disk, re-scoring is a load and a predict.

### The result

Fitted on every character through October 2008, scored on November 2008:

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows scored | 12,603 |
| Actual churn rate | 0.604 |
| Predicted churn rate | 0.646 |
| **ROC AUC** | **0.8324** |

That is below the 0.8817 the same configuration scores in cross-validation, and
the gap is expected rather than a bug. The cross-validation number is a mean over
30 folds inside the historical window; this is a single month from a different
period, and November's churn rate (0.60) is far above the ~0.36 the model was
trained around. A shifted base rate is exactly the situation where a ranking
metric degrades.

The configuration is in `reports/final_config.json` and the fitted learner in
`reports/final_learner.joblib`, so the run is reproducible without re-running the
search.

January 2009 stops on the 10th because that is where the dataset ends. That caps
the last *usable* target at December 2008 — a January row's label would need
February's data to be observed — but December's own label is `churn` in January,
and a character who played on January 11th or later is recorded as absent. The
label is therefore wrong for those characters, so the unseen evaluation reports
November only.

## Reading the execution report

Every `evaluate()` run writes a skrub report to `reports/execution_report/`. It
is the easiest way to inspect the plan: the graph itself, per-node timing, and
the fitted state of each transformer. Open
`reports/execution_report/index.html` in a browser.

The node that dominates the runtime is the location block, which is why it is a
choice rather than a fixed part of the plan.

## Data quality and quirks

Several decisions in the code are responses to data problems that are easy to
miss when reading the table:

- `guild == -1` means "no guild" and is mapped to null in `make_data_op`.
- Duplicate heartbeats at the same timestamp exist, and show up as the `0s
  (duplicate)` bar in the gap histogram.
- The level cap moves: 60 → 70 in April 2007, 70 → 80 in November 2008. Any
  level-based feature is therefore not comparable across the whole window.
- Expansion releases are a confounder: they cause both an influx of characters
  and a change in behaviour.

## Reproducing the post

The `pixi` tasks and the `main.py` CLI are the entry points:

```bash
# Evaluate the plan on the historical window
pixi run python main.py --env train --fraction 0.1

# Run one search stage
pixi run python main.py --env train --fraction 0.1 --stage capacity \
    --search --n-iter 60 --study-name wowah_churn_capacity \
    --frozen '{"session_gap": 60, "lags": [1,2,3], ...}'

# Fit on every character and save the learner
pixi run python main.py --env fit-final --fraction 1 \
    --frozen '{"session_gap": 60, "lags": [1,2,3], ...}'

# Load the saved learner and score November 2008
pixi run python main.py --env score-unseen
```

`run_stages.py` chains the stages, carrying each winner into the next:

```bash
pixi run python run_stages.py --stages gaps structural capacity
```

`explore_data.py` regenerates the exploration figures. Determinism is partial:
`sample_by_user` uses `seed=42`, but the model is not seeded, so AUC varies by a
few hundredths between runs. With the parquet source a 10% trial takes about two
minutes; the full-data fit takes about the same, because the parse is no longer
the bottleneck.

The search runs sequentially. Parallel trials are not offered: parsing spawns a
process pool sized to the core count, so N workers on a cold cache means N ×
cores processes, and eight workers drove a 24 GB machine into 40 GB of swap.

## Caching the plan

Parsing the raw logs is the most expensive thing in the project, and the way the
pipeline is evaluated makes it worse than it looks. This section is about the one
line of configuration that fixes it, and about the trap that makes the fix
dangerous if you forget it.

### The parse is a node, and the node runs 63 times

`load` is not a preprocessing step that happens before the pipeline starts. It is
a node of the plan, sitting at the top of the graph:

```python
raw_files = skrub.var("raw_files")
historical_data = raw_files.skb.apply_func(load, fraction=load_fraction)
```

That is deliberate — it is what lets the same graph be fitted on the historical
files and later run on files it has never seen. But it also means the parse is
re-executed every time the plan is evaluated, and `cross_validate` evaluates the
plan **once per fit and once per score**:

$$30 \text{ folds} \times 2 + 1 = 61 \text{ evaluations}$$

Each evaluation parses all 138,084 historical heartbeat files. A single parse
takes **68 s** and returns 36.5M rows, so an uncached cross-validation spends
about **69 minutes parsing alone** — before any feature engineering or model
fitting.

### One line turns it off

skrub's Data Ops cache is a single configuration call:

```python
CACHE_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / ".skrub_cache"
skrub.set_config(cache=str(CACHE_DIR))
```

With it on, the first evaluation parses and every later one reuses the result.
Measured end to end at `load_fraction=0.1`:

| | wall time | `parse_files` calls |
|---|---:|---:|
| cache off | ~69 min (extrapolated) | 61 |
| cache cold | 289 s | 1 |
| cache warm | 213 s | 0 |

The cache-off figure is extrapolated rather than measured: an uncached
`cross_validate` was still running after 30 minutes and was stopped. The 61-call
count and the 68 s per-call cost were both measured directly, by memoizing the
parse so the count could be taken without paying 61 × 68 s.

### Two different savings, often confused

The table hides two separate effects, and they are not the same size:

- **cache off → cache on**: 63 parses become 1. About **15× faster**. This is
  the one that matters.
- **cache cold → cache warm**: 1 parse becomes 0. 289 s → 213 s, about **26%**.
  Modest, because the remaining time is model fitting and encoding, not parsing.

So "the cache makes the run 26% faster" is true and misleading. The cache is the
difference between a run you can iterate on and a run you leave overnight. The
26% is what you get on the second run of the day.

### The trap: the cache does not know your code changed

joblib keys a cached call on the **cached function's own source** plus its
arguments. It does not look at the functions that function calls. So editing
`adding_features.py` would leave `build_feature_table`'s cache key unchanged, and
the cache would keep serving the old feature table — silently, with no warning,
and with results that look plausible.

The workaround is to put the dependency back into the key by passing a source
fingerprint as an extra argument:

```python
def _source_fingerprint(*modules):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    for module in modules:
        digest.update(Path(module.__file__).read_bytes())
    return digest.hexdigest()[:16]


FEATURES_FINGERPRINT = _source_fingerprint(
    sys.modules[__name__],
    sys.modules["add_churn"],
    sys.modules["adding_features"],
)
```

`build_feature_table` accepts `_fingerprint=None` and immediately does
`del _fingerprint`: the argument exists only to change the cache key, and never
reaches the computation.

| Node | Fingerprinted? | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `load` | no | parser is frozen |
| `build_feature_table` | yes | `main.py`, `add_churn.py`, `adding_features.py` |

The parse node is deliberately left out. The parser is frozen, so the guard would
only ever fire on a change that is not going to happen — and the cost of leaving
it out is that editing `src/parse_to_single_table.py` is not detected. That is a
tidiness trade-off, not a correctness one: delete `.skrub_cache/` by hand if you
ever change the parser.

**If you add a module that `build_feature_table` calls, add it to the
`_source_fingerprint(...)` call.** Otherwise edits to it will be ignored.

### What the cache costs

The cache directory is **587 MB** and git-ignored. It is regenerated on demand,
so deleting it is always safe — it just costs a full recompute, which is the ~75
minutes above. That is the price of changing the parser, or of clearing the cache
to be sure you are not looking at stale features.

### The unseen environment gets its own entry

The cache is keyed on the arguments of the cached call, and `raw_files` is one of
them. The training and unseen environments pass different file lists, so they get
separate cache entries and neither invalidates the other.

The unseen set is much smaller — 10,058 files, 2.31M rows, **7.3 s** to parse —
so caching matters far less there. `fit_final` fits on the historical files and
then parses the unseen ones once; the cache saves that single parse on a repeat
run and nothing more.

### Skipping the parse entirely

Caching makes the parse happen once. Reading a pre-parsed file makes it happen
never, and that is what the searches actually use.

`build_parquet.py` writes the whole corpus to `data/wowah_data_all.parquet` by
calling `parse_files` itself, so the two cannot drift. `make_data_op` then takes
a `source` argument: `"parquet"` reads that file, `"raw"` parses the `.txt`
files. Both go through the same code, so the choice does not change any result.

Measured on the same configuration at a 10% sample:

| Source | Wall time | AUC |
|---|---:|---:|
| `parquet` | 208 s | 0.8724 |
| `raw` | 323 s | 0.8734 |

The parquet is also a strict **superset** of what `list_raw_files` returns. A
heartbeat at 23:57 is stored in the *next* day's folder, so filtering by folder
name drops it while the parquet keeps it. That is the whole of the 0.001 AUC
difference, and it is the reason the parquet is the default.

Regenerate it whenever the parser changes:

```bash
pixi run python build_parquet.py
```

## Limitations and what would come next

- **Right-censoring.** Characters still active at the end of the window have no
  observed churn, and the last months are dropped entirely. A survival-analysis
  framing (time-to-churn) would use those rows instead of throwing them away.
- **Avatars are treated as players.** A player with several avatars is counted
  several times, and churn on one avatar is not churn on the player.
- **No causal claim.** The model says who is at risk, not whether an incentive
  would have worked.
- **Monthly granularity is a choice.** Weekly would give more folds but a noisier
  label.
